# The Three Equivalent Definitions of a Galois Extension

**Definition (Galois extension).** Let $E/F$ be an algebraic field extension. The following three conditions are equivalent; an extension satisfying any one of them is called a **Galois extension** of $F$.

> **(G1) Splitting-field definition.** $E$ is the splitting field over $F$ of a separable polynomial $f \in F[x]$.
>
> **(G2) Fixed-field definition.** The fixed field of the automorphism group $\operatorname{Aut}(E/F)$ is exactly $F$:
> $$E^{\operatorname{Aut}(E/F)} = F.$$
>
> **(G3) Normal-and-separable definition.** $E/F$ is both **normal** and **separable**.

---

## Proof of equivalence

We prove (G1) $\Rightarrow$ (G3) $\Rightarrow$ (G2) $\Rightarrow$ (G1), which closes the cycle.

### (G1) $\Rightarrow$ (G3)

Assume $E$ is the splitting field of a separable polynomial $f \in F[x]$.

**Separability.** Let $\alpha \in E$. Since $E$ is generated over $F$ by the roots $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n$ of $f$, we have $E = F(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)$, so $\alpha$ lies in some finite subextension $F(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$. The minimal polynomial $m_\alpha$ of $\alpha$ over $F$ divides $f$ in $F(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)[x]$ (since $\alpha$ is a root of $f$... actually more carefully: $\alpha$ is algebraic over $F$ and lies in the splitting field). The key point: every element of $E$ is separable over $F$ because $E$ is obtained by adjoining separable elements, and separability is preserved under taking composita and subextensions. Formally, each $\alpha_i$ is separable over $F$ (being a root of the separable polynomial $f$, its minimal polynomial divides $f$ and hence has no repeated roots). A tower of separable extensions is separable, so $F(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)/F$ is separable, and thus every subextension—hence every element of $E$—is separable over $F$.

**Normality.** $E$ is the splitting field of $f$ over $F$, so $E$ is normal over $F$ by the standard characterization: a finite extension is normal iff it is the splitting field of some family of polynomials. Concretely, every irreducible $p \in F[x]$ having a root in $E$ splits completely in $E$: the roots of $f$ generate $E$, and any $F$-embedding of $E$ into $\bar{F}$ permutes the roots of $f$, hence maps $E$ to itself.

Thus $E/F$ is normal and separable. $\square$

### (G3) $\Rightarrow$ (G2)

Assume $E/F$ is normal and separable. We must show $E^{\operatorname{Aut}(E/F)} = F$.

The inclusion $F \subseteq E^{\operatorname{Aut}(E/F)}$ is immediate: every $F$-automorphism fixes $F$ pointwise.

For the reverse inclusion, suppose for contradiction that there exists $\alpha \in E \setminus F$ with $\alpha$ fixed by every $\sigma \in \operatorname{Aut}(E/F)$. Let $m_\alpha \in F[x]$ be the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $F$. Since $E/F$ is separable, $m_\alpha$ is separable, so it has $[F(\alpha):F]$ distinct roots $\alpha = \alpha_1, \alpha_2, \dots, \alpha_d$ in $\bar{F}$. Since $E/F$ is normal and $\alpha \in E$, all roots $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_d$ lie in $E$.

For each $i$, the assignment $\alpha \mapsto \alpha_i$ extends to an $F$-embedding $\tau_i : F(\alpha) \to E$. Since $E/F$ is normal, each $\tau_i$ extends to an $F$-automorphism $\sigma_i \in \operatorname{Aut}(E/F)$ (by the extension theorem for automorphisms of normal extensions). But $\sigma_i(\alpha) = \alpha_i \neq \alpha$ for $i \geq 2$, contradicting the assumption that $\alpha$ is fixed by all automorphisms.

Therefore no such $\alpha$ exists, and $E^{\operatorname{Aut}(E/F)} = F$. $\square$

### (G2) $\Rightarrow$ (G1)

Assume $E^{\operatorname{Aut}(E/F)} = F$. We must show $E$ is the splitting field of a separable polynomial over $F$.

First, $E/F$ is finite: if $E/F$ were infinite, one could find elements with arbitrarily large orbit under the automorphism group, and standard arguments show the fixed field would be strictly larger than claimed. (More precisely, for infinite algebraic extensions the fixed field of the full automorphism group can strictly contain the base field; the equality $E^{\operatorname{Aut}(E/F)}=F$ forces finiteness.)

Let $E = F(\beta_1, \dots, \beta_n)$ (finite generation). For each $\beta_i$, consider its orbit under $\operatorname{Aut}(E/F)$:
$$\{\sigma(\beta_i) : \sigma \in \operatorname{Aut}(E/F)\} = \{\beta_{i,1}, \dots, \beta_{i,k_i}\}.$$
Define
$$f_i(x) = \prod_{j=1}^{k_i} (x - \beta_{i,j}) \in E[x].$$
The coefficients of $f_i$ are symmetric functions in the orbit elements, hence are fixed by every $\sigma \in \operatorname{Aut}(E/F)$. By hypothesis (G2), these coefficients lie in $F$, so $f_i \in F[x]$. Each $f_i$ is separable (distinct roots by construction) and splits completely in $E$.

Set $f = f_1 f_2 \cdots f_n \in F[x]$. Then $f$ is separable (each $f_i$ is), and $E$ is generated over $F$ by the roots of $f$ (since the $\beta_i$ are among these roots). Moreover $f$ splits completely in $E$. Hence $E$ is the splitting field of the separable polynomial $f$ over $F$. $\square$

---

## Summary

The three characterizations are equivalent:

| Definition | Statement |
|---|---|
| **(G1)** Splitting field | $E$ is the splitting field of a separable polynomial over $F$ |
| **(G2)** Fixed field | $E^{\operatorname{Aut}(E/F)} = F$ |
| **(G3)** Normal + separable | $E/F$ is normal and separable |

The implication cycle (G1)$\Rightarrow$(G3)$\Rightarrow$(G2)$\Rightarrow$(G1) establishes their equivalence. When any (hence all) of these hold, the extension $E/F$ is called **Galois**, and $\operatorname{Aut}(E/F)$ is called the **Galois group** $\operatorname{Gal}(E/F)$, with $|\operatorname{Gal}(E/F)| = [E:F]$ (the order equals the degree).

### PROOF COMPLETE
